title: 👑 Elite Challenge ⭐⭐⭐⭐: choosing the right past

questions.explanation: In the simple past negative, "did not" carries the past and the verb goes back to its base form: She didn't know the answer. ✓ The trap is to keep the irregular past form after didn't ("didn't knew") — the past is then marked twice. "She not knew" forgets "did", and "hasn't knew" puts a simple past where the present perfect needs the participle "known".

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the present perfect to talk about a CHANGE between the past and now?

options.text: Our village has become a big town.
Our village became a town in 1990.
Have you ever seen our village?
The mayor has just opened a park.

questions.explanation: A change compares the past and now: "Our village has become a big town" (it was small, now it is big) — present perfect, has + past participle. ✓ "Have you ever seen…?" is also present perfect, but it asks about an experience, and "has just opened" gives a piece of news. "became a town in 1990" has a finished time, so it is simple past.

questions.prompt: Complete with ONE word: "We have seen a lot of tourists in our town ___."
questions.explanation: "lately" means "in the last days or weeks", goes with the present perfect and comes at the end of the sentence: We have seen a lot of tourists lately. ✓ "just" also goes with the present perfect, but its place is between have and the participle (have just seen), never at the end. "yesterday" is a finished time that needs the simple past, and "ago" needs a period before it (two days ago).

questions.prompt: Complete: "I first ___ snails in 2019, and I ___ them a lot lately."
questions.explanation: Each part of the sentence has its own time. "in 2019" is finished, so simple past: I first ate snails in 2019. "lately" goes with the present perfect: I have eaten them a lot lately. ✓ The trap is to use one tense for the whole sentence: "have eaten" is impossible with "in 2019", and "ate" does not go with "lately".

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes an action IN PROGRESS at a moment in the past?

options.text: Right now, the volunteers are cleaning the beach.
At six, the volunteers were cleaning the beach.
The volunteers have just cleaned the beach.
Last Sunday, the volunteers cleaned the whole beach.

questions.explanation: The past progressive (was/were + verb + ing) describes a past action in progress: at six, the cleaning was going on — the volunteers were cleaning the beach. ✓ "are cleaning" is also in progress, but now, not in the past. "cleaned the whole beach" tells a completed action (simple past), and "have just cleaned" gives a very recent result (present perfect).

questions.prompt: Choose the correct set of verbs: "Yesterday at five, Mum ___ dinner and my sisters ___ their homework. Then Dad ___ home."

options.text: was cooking / were doing / has come

questions.explanation: At five the two actions were in progress, so past progressive: "Mum" is she → was cooking; "my sisters" are they → were doing. Dad's arrival is a completed action in a finished past (yesterday), so simple past: came. ✓ The traps: "was doing" with my sisters and "were cooking" with Mum break the was/were agreement, and "has come" puts the present perfect in a finished time.
